hero.caption:
c/n BA-111
Built in 1955, this E.18 was used as a corporate transport in the US until 1964 when it flew to the UK and was modified for surveying work which included fitting a transparent nose cone. It joined Survey Flights Ltd in Northern Island who operated it until 1968, when it joined the Scottish Airline Loganair.
Converted to a nine-seat passenger layout, it then operated the airlines passenger and newspaper routes. In July 1969 it carried out the airlines first international service when it flew from Glasgow to Stavanger, Norway, via Aberdeen. During its time with Loganair it also served as an Air Ambulance, due to its long range capability.
It was retired in March 1975 due to the cost of an upcoming wingspar inspection, but by March 1976 it had been safely preserved as part of the Scottish national collection.
It is currently on display in the Civil Aviation Hangar at the National Museum of Flight (part of National Museums Scotland).
East Fortune Airfield, East Lothian, Scotland.

13th September 2017.

Built 1954.
Originally registered to the Ministry of Transport and Civil Aviation, it passed through the Board of Trade and the Secretary of State before ending up with the Civil Aviation Authority in 1972. It operated from Stansted on calibration and licensing flights before being deregistered in 1981.
In genuine CAA markings, it is on display in the Civil Aviation Hangar at the National Museum of Flight (part of National Museums Scotland).
East Fortune Airfield, East Lothian, Scotland.

images.caption:
BAC / Aerospatiale Concorde 102 ‘G-BOAA’
c/n 206.
‘Alpha Alpha’ first flew on 5th November 1975 and was the first Concorde delivered to British Airways, which took place on 14th January 1976. On 21st January she flew the very first British Airways Concorde service, which was from London to Bahrain.
During her service career she flew 22,768 hours and carried out 8,064 landings. Between January 1979 and July 1980 she was registered as ‘G-N94AA / N94AA’ as part of a joint venture with Braniff.
Her last flight was on 12th August 2000, a return flight from New York JFK to her home at London Heathrow. In 2004 she was dismantled and moved by road and sea to East Fortune in Scotland. Fully reassembled, she has become a focal point and headline item for the museum.  Surrounded by informative displays and open for viewing, she is on display as ‘The Concorde Experience’ in Hangar 4 as part of the National Museum of Flight, part of National Museums Scotland.
East Fortune Airfield, East Lothian, Scotland.

13th September 2017.

images.caption:
c/n 227
Originally built by Handley Page in 1969 as an HP137 Jetstream Mk.1 with the registration G-AXJZ. It was immediately exported to America but returned to the UK in 1979 under the ownership of British Aerospace. In 1980 it flew as the prototype Jetstream 3100, more commonly known as the Jetstream 31. It was used as a demonstrator until roughly 1990 when it was stored at Prestwick before joining Scotland’s National collection. 
On display in Hangar 4 at the National Museum of Flight (part of National Museums Scotland).
East Fortune Airfield, East Lothian, Scotland.

13th September 2017.

images.caption:
c/n 2108.
Built 1964 and flew for British European Airways (BEA) until January 1974 when the merger with British Overseas Airways Corporation (BOAC) created British Airways. Continued to operate with British Airways until retired and by 1982 was on display at the Cosford Aerospace Museum as part of the British Airways collection. When the collection was dissolved, a combination of corrosion and transport costs sadly meant that the Trident, along with Vickers VC10 ‘G-ARVM’ and Boeing 707 ‘G-APFJ’, were too expensive to save and in early 2006 they were broken up on site. While the fuselage of the VC10 is now at Brooklands, most of the other aircraft and remains, including the complete Viscount and BAC-111, moved to East Fortune. The Trident was reduced to just this cockpit section, which is now on display in Hangar 4 at the National Museum of Flight (part of National Museums Scotland).
East Fortune Airfield, East Lothian, Scotland.

13th September 2017.

images.caption:
c/n 17711, l/n 163.
Built 1960 and flew for British Overseas Airways Corporation (BOAC). In November 1971 she was leased to Malaysia-Singapore Airlines (MSA), returning in April 1975 to what had then become British Airways, after the 1974 merger with British European Airways (BEA). 
She continued to operate with British Airways, and subsidiary ‘British Airtours’ until retired and put on display at the Cosford Aerospace Museum as part of the British Airways collection. When the collection was dissolved, a combination of corrosion and transport costs sadly meant that the last surviving Conway powered 707, along with Vickers VC10 ‘G-ARVM’ and Trident 1C ‘G-ARPH’, were too expensive to save and in early 2006 they were broken up on site. While the fuselage of the VC10 is now at Brooklands, most of the other aircraft and remains, including the complete Viscount and BAC-111, moved to East Fortune. The 707 was also reduced to a fuselage section and this is now on display, repainted in gorgeous BOAC livery and filled with fascinating displays and information, in Hangar 4 at the National Museum of Flight (part of National Museums Scotland).
East Fortune Airfield, East Lothian, Scotland.

13th September 2017.

images.caption: The Museum of Flight. This Museum is housed in the hangars which were a part of the RAF base at East Fortune which operated during the First and Second world wars. The base was also used in 1919 as the point of departure of the R34 airship which set off from there on its record breaking trip across the Atlantic. The museum opened in 1975 and now houses one of the retired Concordes.

images.caption: On the night of 2nd-3rd April 1916, two German Navy Zeppelins, failing to find their intended target, Rosyth Dockyard, dropped 27 bombs on Leith and Edinburgh instead. This one failed to explode. East Fortune airfield was alerted when the first Zeppelin was spotted coming in over the Berwickshire coast and sent up one aeroplane to intercept. Owing to poor visibility, it failed to locate the intruders and crash landed on return.

images.filename: Wing frame from Sopwith Cuckoo – East Fortune. 13-9-2017 (39811881972).jpg
images.caption:
The Sopwith T.1 Cuckoo was a biplane torpedo bomber which entered service with the Royal Naval Air Service (RNAS) in 1918 and served until 1923, by which time the RNAS had become part of the Royal Air Force.
Only 232 Cuckoos were built and there are no surviving examples.
This wing frame is on display in the ‘Fortunes of War’ building at the National Museum of Flight (part of National Museums Scotland).
East Fortune Airfield, East Lothian, Scotland.

13th September 2017
